issues.description:
Empty mail headers consume the following field. mobile/src/services/mail/imapFetchBody.ts:33-52 uses \s* after the colon, which also matches a newline. Reproduction: parseHeaderField("Subject:
From: alice@example.com

Body", "Subject") returns "From: alice@example.com" instead of an empty string. This misrepresents message metadata, and applies to From/To/Date as well. Restrict whitespace to spaces/tabs and unfold only continuation lines. Confirmed by issue_tracker/review_checks.mjs.

Failed IMAP FETCH can be reported as successful. mobile/src/services/mail/imapFetchBody.ts:67-71 accepts a tagged completion whenever the entire line includes " OK", instead of checking the status atom. Reproduction: a BODY[] payload followed by "a1 NO server says OK later" returns the payload instead of rejecting the failed command. Check an anchored tagged OK status, case-insensitively, as readHeaderRecords already does. Confirmed by issue_tracker/review_checks.mjs.

MIME text decoding ignores the declared charset. mobile/src/services/mail/mime.ts:55-83 and collectFromEntity decode all base64/quoted-printable text as UTF-8 without reading the Content-Type charset parameter. Reproduction: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-8859-1 plus base64 Y2Fm6Q== renders caf followed by a replacement character instead of café. Separate transfer decoding into bytes from charset decoding and handle supported declared encodings explicitly. Confirmed by issue_tracker/review_checks.mjs.

Valid SMTP RCPT success replies cause send to wait until timeout. mobile/src/services/mail/smtp.ts:16-34 and sendMimeMessage RCPT loop accept only 250; RFC 5321 also allows 251 (forwarding) and 252 for RCPT. A server replying "251 User not local; will forward" has completed the response, but readSmtpUntil keeps reading while the server waits for DATA. The message is not submitted. Accept the command-specific success set and fail promptly on unexpected completed replies. Confirmed with a scripted client in issue_tracker/review_checks.mjs; real sockets eventually raise TCP readLine timed out.

Message detail extraction repeatedly scans and normalizes the entire mail source for headers. mobile/src/services/mail/imapFetchBody.ts:19-25 normalizes all CRLF/CR characters before locating the header boundary; messageDetailFromRfc822:112-115 calls that path four times for Subject/From/To/Date. Thus large message bodies and attachments are traversed repeatedly even though only a short header block is needed. Extract the header block once before normalization and parse all fields from it. Verified by tracing the four calls and the two replace operations per call; no runtime speedup estimate claimed.

Strict JSON validation builds and discards a sorted deep copy. core/StrictJson.ts:40 calls canonicalize(value) solely for validation and returns the original value. core/CanonicalJson.ts canonicalize recursively allocates new objects/arrays and sorts every object key, so every strict parse pays for another full object graph and key sorting whose result is unused. Add a validation-only traversal with the same string/number rules; keep copying/sorting only where a caller actually needs it. Verified by code inspection of both functions; performance impact grows with payload size.

Duplicate RFC822 header parsers already use different rules. mobile/src/services/mail/imapFetchBody.ts:19-52 implements boundary detection/unfolding/field extraction, while mobile/src/services/mail/mime.ts:14-37 implements another parser with its own normalization, duplicate-header and continuation rules. One handles bare CR and the other does not; field extraction also has the empty-header bug recorded separately. Maintaining separate parsers makes it difficult to reason about which headers drive display versus MIME processing and requires fixes in multiple places. Extract one shared, explicitly specified header parser with tests for empty fields, folding, duplicate fields and line endings.

Strict JSON scanner obscures its cursor invariants and trust in JSON.parse. core/StrictJson.ts:8-37 packs delimiter advances, whitespace handling, recursion and early returns onto single lines, uses a helper named string, and advances past colons/commas without explaining that the initial JSON.parse has already validated grammar. This security-sensitive duplicate-key check is difficult to audit or debug when escaped keys or nested structures fail. Expand each state transition, use descriptive helper names and document the valid-input precondition and cursor positions; preserve duplicate escaped-name checks in focused tests. This is an auditability concern, not a demonstrated incorrect parse.

Quoted display names containing commas create invalid recipient chips and block sending. Locations: common/ComposeRecipients.ts:38-73 (parseAddressList), gui/js/compose-recipients-logic.js:5-33 (GUI mirror), gui/js/compose-recipients.js:94-99 (addFromText), and mobile/src/services/mail/recipientChipsLogic.ts:70-82 (appendAddresses). The parser splits on every comma before unwrapping Name <address>, without respecting quoted display names. Reproduction against both actual implementations: parseAddressList('"Doe, Jane" <jane@example.com>') returns [{email:'"Doe',valid:false},{email:'jane@example.com',valid:true}] instead of one valid jane@example.com recipient. deriveComposeIntent with the first chip invalid returns blocked, even when the valid address is explicitly plaintext. Pasting this valid mailbox representation therefore adds a spurious invalid recipient that the user must remove before sending. Node 24 type stripping and VM evaluation reproduced the actual functions; all existing shared parse/intent fixtures passed in both implementations. UI callers were traced by inspection; no interactive GUI/mobile session was run. This is independent of the previously recorded RFC822 message-header parser issues. Reviewed commit: 587a8873ac613507a4d180b67b7f85ea02cfcb6d.

Payment reconciliation repeats global expiry updates for every order in a batch. Locations: server/handlers/mail-payment.ts:449-473 (reconcilePendingPayments), server/handlers/mail-payment.ts:255-256 (handlePaymentOrder), and server/payments/orders.ts:118-131 (expirePaymentOrders). Reconciliation expires orders once, selects up to 50 pending orders, then calls handlePaymentOrder separately for each. That handler repeats expirePaymentOrders, which executes two unscoped-by-order UPDATE statements over eligible quoted/pending orders. A full batch consequently issues 2 + 50*2 = 102 global expiry UPDATE statements, in addition to per-order reads, timestamp writes and provider checks. server/main.ts:52-59 schedules batches every 30 seconds while preventing timer overlap; the overlap guard does not remove this redundant work. Verified by Node 24 type-stripped evaluation of the actual reconciliation, handler and expiry functions: a counting database stub returned 50 valid order IDs and pending orders with unavailable configuration; exactly 102 expiry UPDATE calls occurred. Provider calls were not needed because expiry happens before configuration checking. This establishes repeated database calls and avoidable write-statement/round-trip overhead as pending volume grows, not a measured speedup or a claim that each query scans the whole table. Reviewed commit: 587a8873ac613507a4d180b67b7f85ea02cfcb6d.

Background payment failures discard the context needed to diagnose individual orders. Locations: server/handlers/mail-payment.ts:275-279 and 334-340 (different verification failure responses), and server/handlers/mail-payment.ts:464-481 (reconcilePendingPayments response handling). The background worker routes each order through an HTTP handler, logs only 'payment reconciliation returned HTTP <status>' for non-OK responses, and cancels the response body without reading its error. Neither that log nor the catch log includes the orderId already available in the loop. Configuration unavailable and provider-verification failures both surface as HTTP 503, so operators cannot associate a failure with an order or distinguish these causes from the worker output. This is a concrete debugging/maintenance obstacle for a background workflow processing up to 50 payments, distinct from its repeated expiry queries. Reproduced with actual type-stripped reconciliation and handler functions, a 50-order database stub, missing payment configuration and captured console.error: all 50 messages were exactly 'payment reconciliation returned HTTP 503', with no order ID or response reason. Provider-error convergence and response-body cancellation were additionally confirmed by source inspection; no live chain service was used. Reviewed commit: 587a8873ac613507a4d180b67b7f85ea02cfcb6d.

Contact refresh retains stale opaque-email resolutions and treats them as current identity claims. Locations: gui/local-backend/contacts.ts:148-155 (saveExternalContact), mobile/src/services/contacts.ts:196-205 (importContact), common/MailAuthenticity.ts:113-123 and 162-165 (resolved claim matching and verification metadata), and mobile/src/services/contactsLogic.ts:162-164 (contactMatchesEmail). Both contact save paths preserve resolvedOpaqueDetails entries whenever the incoming details map still contains that path, without checking whether its hash changed or still hashes to the preserved cleartext. Reproduction: save a contact whose opaque::email was SHA256(old@example.com), locally resolved to old@example.com; refresh the same contact with opaque::email set to SHA256(new@example.com). The stored resolution remains old@example.com. resolveSignerEmailClaim(refreshedContact, 'old@example.com') reports signerMatchesSenderEmail=true; with verified metadata on the new opaque claim it also reports signerEmailVerified=true, although the current hash does not commit to the old address. Mobile contactMatchesEmail likewise returns true for the stale address, allowing local recipient resolution to select this identity after its published email changes. Confirmed by executing actual Node 24 type-stripped GUI save, mobile import, shared authenticity, and mobile matching functions with an in-memory filesystem and real SHA-256. Synthetic public-key/proof fields and metadata were supplied to isolate refresh and matching; cryptographic signing, server endorsement and UI flows were not exercised. The demonstrated defect is stale claim association, not a signature forgery. Reviewed commit: 758b19bac1ef700a58baf89a9a396c552c0ae050.

One malformed contact file aborts contact listing and can hide unrelated healthy contacts from fingerprint lookup. Locations: gui/local-backend/contacts.ts:17-35 (loadContact fallback scan), gui/local-backend/contacts.ts:44-62 (listContacts), and mobile/src/services/contacts.ts:60-78 (listContacts). JSON parsing and record reads have no per-entry isolation: a malformed unrelated .json file rejects the entire list, and the GUI prefix scan exits before reaching later valid contacts. A truncated local file after an interrupted non-atomic contact write is one realistic trigger; GUI saveExternalContact:167 and mobile importContact:211 write directly to the destination. Reproduction with an in-memory contact directory ordered broken.json containing '{', followed by alice.json containing a healthy identity: GUI listContacts, mobile listContacts, and GUI loadContact(ctx, 'test-finger') for alice's fingerprint all reject with SyntaxError. Removing the broken entry makes the healthy record reachable. Actual functions ran under Node 24 type stripping with filesystem APIs stubbed; no real crash or disk corruption was induced. This lets one damaged record disable whole-directory operations and dependent recipient discovery rather than limiting the failure to that record. Direct lookup by a healthy exact alias can still succeed; not all contact access is affected. Reviewed commit: 758b19bac1ef700a58baf89a9a396c552c0ae050.

Base64 encoding builds a per-byte concatenation chain with high transient heap use on supported file inputs. Locations: core/Base64.ts:2-7 (bytesToBase64), core/FilePayload.ts:37-48 (createFileCleartextEnvelope), cli/commands/files.ts:33-38 (file encryption input/envelope), and common/FileLimits.ts:2 (25 MiB supported file limit). bytesToBase64 appends one one-character string for every input byte before calling btoa, retaining a large intermediate string structure in addition to the input and encoded output. Isolated Node 24.22.1 reproduction: load the actual type-stripped function in a VM, allocate a 4,194,304-byte Uint8Array filled with 65, force GC before the call, and compare process.memoryUsage().heapUsed before and immediately after. Encoding produced the correct 5,592,408-character Base64 output, equal to Buffer.from(input).toString('base64'), but heapUsed increased by 139,797,912 bytes (about 133 MiB). This input is below the application's 25 MiB limit. The measurement is one Node/V8 run, includes uncollected transient allocations, and is neither retained heap after GC nor a mobile-engine benchmark; no universal memory multiplier or speedup is claimed. The actual file-envelope call path demonstrates this cost is relevant to normal file encryption, beyond tiny public keys and signatures. Reviewed commit: 758b19bac1ef700a58baf89a9a396c552c0ae050.

Empty email attachment envelopes cannot round-trip through the shared writer and reader. Locations: core/EmailAttachmentPayload.ts:50-67 (createEmailAttachmentCleartextEnvelope) and :94-100 (parseEmailAttachmentCleartextEnvelope). The writer accepts a zero-length Uint8Array and emits fileSize=0 and fileDataBase64='', but the reader requires a nonempty Base64 string even though fileSize validation permits zero. Reproduction: createEmailAttachmentCleartextEnvelope({attachmentId:'id',fileBytes:new Uint8Array(),fileName:'empty.txt'}), JSON.stringify the result, then pass it to parseEmailAttachmentCleartextEnvelope: it throws 'Invalid email attachment envelope fileDataBase64'. A one-byte attachment succeeds as a control. Actual functions were evaluated with Node 24 type stripping, actual Base64 helpers/version constants, and JSON.parse substituted for the strict parser on these well-formed generated envelopes. This is a core API serialization inconsistency for legitimate empty files. The GUI input validator in route-support.ts also rejects empty Base64, so this does not establish that the current GUI can send a zero-byte attachment; it establishes rejection rather than round-trip support at both boundaries. No encryption or network traffic was involved. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

Concurrent local hierarchy proposal additions overwrite each other and return duplicate IDs. Locations: gui/local-backend/hierarchy-local.ts:89-131 (readPendingHierarchyLocal, writePendingHierarchyLocal, addPendingHierarchyLocal) and gui/local-backend/hierarchy-routes.ts:144-151 (proposal route). addPendingHierarchyLocal independently reads the entire queue, computes max(id)+1, appends, and writes the whole file, without a queue or lock spanning that read-modify-write operation. Two overlapping proposals in separate tabs or requests can both read the same initial state and each report success, while the last write drops the other proposal. Reproduction: Promise.all two actual addPendingHierarchyLocal calls on an initially absent queue, with the same master and distinct children. Both returned id=1; readPendingHierarchyLocal afterward contained only one of the two children. Node 24 type-stripped functions used an asynchronous in-memory filesystem; no real disk corruption or server was involved. The route awaits this helper but has no cross-request serialization. Server-side database transaction protection does not serialize the local JSON queue. When server publication is unavailable, which the route intentionally tolerates, the overwritten proposal has no reliable local persistence. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

GUI contact aliases are interpolated into filesystem paths without directory containment. Locations: gui/local-backend/contacts-routes.ts:40-65 and :90-92 (contact import), and gui/local-backend/contacts.ts:102-105 (deleteContact by name). The import route validates the contact fingerprint but accepts any string alias, appends '.json', and passes contactsDir/name.json directly to Deno.writeTextFile. Reproduction of the actual import handler with contactsDir='/safe/contacts', name='../victim', and an existing '/safe/victim.json': the route returns HTTP 200 and replaces that outside-directory file with contact JSON. Filesystem calls were modeled in memory with POSIX path normalization; fingerprint-format validation was stubbed to accept the synthetic contact, which isolates the alias path independently of fingerprint validity. A real valid contact passes the same branch. The GUI load/delete/save helpers likewise use aliases directly; the CLI has validateContactName, but the GUI does not call it. CSRF/Host/Origin middleware restricts who may call these routes, so this is not an unauthenticated cross-origin exploit. It is a missing filename boundary on an authorized contact operation, allowing an alias containing '..' and separators to overwrite unrelated writable JSON data, potentially including application state. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

Transient mail-vault read errors are treated as empty successful unlocks and permit overwriting existing credentials. Locations: gui/local-backend/mail-account.ts:77-85 (readJsonFile), :260-275 (unlockMailSecretsWithPin), :278-288 (tryUnlockMailSecretsWithIdentityPassword), and :294-311 (saveMailSecretsStore). readJsonFile returns null for every read or JSON error, not just a missing file. unlockMailSecretsWithPin interprets that null as an absent vault, caches an empty store and the supplied password, and reports success. A later save encrypts that empty-derived store over the real existing file. Reproduction using actual functions and real WebCrypto PBKDF2/AES-GCM: create an encrypted vault containing old credentials; simulate a filesystem read error during tryUnlockMailSecretsWithIdentityPassword; it returns true and getMailSecretsStore returns empty. Restore reads, save a new account's credentials, then decrypt the saved vault: the old credentials are gone and only the new account remains. Node 24 evaluated the source with an in-memory filesystem; the read fault was injected, not induced on live storage. This is silent persistent credential loss after a temporary read failure, distinct from a wrong-password error (which correctly rejects) and from issue #13's contact-list error propagation. Invalid JSON is swallowed through the same path, though the executable reproduction used a transient I/O error. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

Saving a GUI mail account with secret persistence disabled discards its passwords from memory immediately. Locations: gui/local-backend/mail-routes.ts:236-267 (account-save branch) and gui/local-backend/mail-account.ts:294-311 and :319-337 (secret-store persistence and account resolution). The route builds nextSecrets and inserts them in secretStore, then deletes that same entry when persistSecrets=false before calling saveMailSecretsStore, which caches the filtered store. The response still reports hasImapPassword/hasSmtpPassword from the deleted nextSecrets object. Reproduction: POST a fresh account with valid IMAP/SMTP configuration, both passwords and persistSecrets=false to the actual handleMailRoutes function. It returns HTTP 200 and both password flags true; immediately calling the actual resolveMailAccount for that identity rejects with 'mail credentials are not configured'. Node 24 type-stripped route and account helpers ran against an in-memory filesystem; identity unlock and context lookup were stubbed successful and no mail server was contacted. Nonpersistent credentials should be usable for the current session while remaining off disk; this path removes them from both. persistSecrets defaults to false, so the failure affects ordinary manual setup without opting into disk storage. Existing account passwords are also removed when switching that account to session-only mode. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

Hierarchy certificate insertion loads every full stored certificate while only using edge fingerprints for graph validation. Locations: server/hierarchy.ts:89-98 (listHierarchyCertificates), :267-277 (verifyAndInsertHierarchyCertificate transaction), and :477 onward (pending proposal validation shares the same global list helper). listHierarchyCertificates selects all eight row columns, including encoded certificate signatures, without filtering the connected component. The insertion path loads them all under the write transaction, maps them to only master_fingerprint and child_fingerprint, then validates that reduced graph. Thus inserting an unrelated edge incurs data transfer and object hydration proportional to the entire certificate archive, including potentially large dual post-quantum signatures that this validation never uses. Reproduction of actual Node 24 type-stripped insertion/list/query-hydration functions with a database stub: return 1,000 rows each containing an 8,192-character certificate; the transaction requests all 1,000 full rows (8,192,000 certificate characters), then passes only 1,000 endpoint pairs into validateHierarchy. Cryptographic verification and graph validation were stubbed to isolate the query/projection; the test stopped at graph validation. The query shape and discarded columns are verified; no live database timing, wire-byte count or speedup is claimed. SQLite's connection queue is held through BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and PostgreSQL takes the shared hierarchy advisory lock, so this unnecessary hydration is also within a serialized write section. This is distinct from existing cycle/concurrency protections, which remain necessary. Reviewed commit: c4724a4a8cd44759b1ad185dca5280aa0acb69e8.

Ethereum checkout retries a non-idempotent send after errors with an unknown broadcast outcome. Locations: website/checkout.js:123-143 (payEthereum). Every eth_sendTransaction error except code 4001 triggers a second eth_sendTransaction with the same value, recipient and message, changing only input to data. This fallback is intended for wallets rejecting the input field, but also covers generic internal/provider errors or response loss after a broadcast. In that case the second request can authorize and send another transfer instead of resolving the first transaction's outcome. Reproduction: execute the actual checkout function with a scripted EIP-1193 provider; the first send records the transaction then rejects with code -32603 and 'response lost after broadcast'; the function issues a second send with identical payment parameters and accepts its returned hash. The simulated wallet records two send requests; the first transaction is not queried or reconciled. No real wallet, signing or chain broadcast was used, so duplicate live transfers are a risk established by the control flow and injected outcome, not an observed on-chain event. Current wallet payment is restricted to native Sepolia ETH for test addresses, which limits financial impact. The existing checkout plan calls for input-compatibility fallback, not blind retry after all non-user-rejection errors. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

Ethereum wallet checkout can send funds from an expired quote before discovering that submission is no longer allowed. Locations: website/checkout-wallet.js:24-57 (walletPayKind and sepoliaPayment), website/checkout.js:123-143 (payEthereum), and server/payments/orders.ts:216-232 (submitPaymentTransaction expiry predicate). Wallet eligibility checks only the cached status, domain, network and asset; it does not inspect expiresAt. A page left open beyond quote expiry retains status='quoted' and an enabled Pay action. payEthereum sends to the wallet before any status refresh or server expiry check; only afterward does it submit the returned hash, which the server refuses once expires_at <= now. Reproduction against actual functions: an otherwise eligible order with expiresAt=1 still has walletPayKind='ethereum'; payEthereum invokes eth_sendTransaction, then rejects after the simulated submission API returns 409. No chain transaction or live API was used. The server's expiry rejection was independently traced to the SQL predicate. This is separate from generic-send retry: one successful send suffices, and the stale quote itself triggers rejection. Current automated wallet payment is testnet-only; nevertheless users can spend test funds and gas on a transfer that cannot be attached through the normal order flow. Cardano's server-side unsigned-transaction path does perform an expiry check. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

Cardano wallet checkout sends all wallet UTxOs into an endpoint that rejects more than 40. Locations: website/checkout.js:145-154 (payCardano) and server/handlers/mail-payment.ts:366 and :390-405 (MAX_WALLET_UTXOS and handleCardanoUnsigned). The browser calls CIP-30 getUtxos with no amount or pagination and forwards the entire result. The server immediately rejects utxos.length > 40 before coin selection. A sufficiently funded preview wallet with 41 or more small outputs therefore cannot use the Pay button even if only a few outputs would cover the quote and fee. Reproduction: a scripted enabled CIP-30 wallet returns network ID 0, a test address and 41 hex UTxO strings; the actual payCardano forwards all 41 to the actual handleCardanoUnsigned count guard, which returns 400 'invalid cardano payment request'. Signing is never reached. Order lookup, request parsing and payability checks were stubbed for a known eligible order; no Lucid transaction construction or real provider was used. The test establishes the browser/server count-contract mismatch, not correctness of synthetic UTxOs or a live wallet balance. The endpoint's bound can remain useful for resource control, but the client currently does nothing to select or request a usable bounded subset. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

An in-flight mobile identity unlock can undo the user's explicit Lock now action. Locations: mobile/src/services/unlockSession.ts:84-91 (lockAll) and :138-151 (cacheUnlockedIdentity), mobile/src/services/storage.ts:199-231 (unlockIdentity), and mobile/src/screens/SettingsScreen.tsx:137-144 (Lock now). cacheUnlockedIdentity waits for asynchronous getAutoLockMinutes before putting the derived key into the store. lockAll clears only sessions that exist at that moment and does not invalidate pending unlock attempts. When the settings read completes, the pending operation unconditionally stores the key and arms a fresh session after the UI has reported 'Identity locked'. Reproduction using actual session-store, settings-parser and unlock-session functions: hold getAutoLockMinutes on a deferred promise, call cacheUnlockedIdentity('alice', key, salt), call lockAll and confirm isUnlocked=false, then resolve the settings promise. The pending unlock completes and isUnlocked becomes true; getKey returns the original nonzero key. Locking after that completion correctly wipes the key as a control. Node 24 type-stripped evaluation used stub React Native AppState and inert timers; no real device or password derivation was used. The actual storage caller passes an already verified/derived key into this same awaited cache path. The timeoutGeneration counter guards timeout preference updates, not cancellation of session creation. This creates a local security-state race rather than a cryptographic bypass. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

Mobile MIME parsing truncates valid quoted boundary parameters containing spaces. Locations: mobile/src/services/mail/mime.ts:38-41 (getBoundary), :129-139 (multipart traversal), and :165-199 (text fallback); mobile/src/services/mail/imap.ts:342-343 (message parsing caller). The boundary regex uses a whitespace-excluding capture even when the parameter is quoted. MIME boundaries may contain internal spaces when quoted, so boundary="valid boundary" is incorrectly extracted as 'valid'. The actual delimiter lines no longer match, no text parts are decoded, and the fallback displays raw multipart syntax and transfer-encoded content instead of the message. Reproduction against actual parser functions: a multipart/mixed message with that quoted boundary and one base64 text/plain part containing aGVsbG8= fails to return 'hello' and instead includes the raw aGVsbG8= body. Changing only the boundary to 'simple' produces 'hello' as a control. Node 24 type-stripped functions used the real Buffer decoder; no mail server or UI was involved. This is independent of issue #3's charset handling and issue #7's duplicate RFC822 header parsers. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

Mobile MIME text extraction merges explicit text attachments into the displayed message body. Locations: mobile/src/services/mail/mime.ts:115-148 (collectFromEntity) and :172-182 (extractTextFromMimeSource), with mobile/src/services/mail/imap.ts:342-343 as the reader call path. Traversal classifies every text/plain or text/html leaf as body text without inspecting Content-Disposition. extractTextFromMimeSource concatenates those leaves, so an attachment marked 'attachment; filename="note.txt"' is presented inline as if authored in the message body. Reproduction: multipart/mixed containing an inline text/plain body 'Message body' and a base64 text/plain attachment containing 'ATTACHMENT TEXT' returns text='Message body

ATTACHMENT TEXT'. Executed the actual functions with Node 24 type stripping and real Buffer decoding; no UI or network session was used. The attachment disposition was explicit, so this is not ambiguity about missing disposition or multipart/alternative preference. The result obscures the boundary between correspondence and separate files, and the same collected parts are also candidates for body EBP-armor extraction, although that downstream effect was inspected rather than reproduced. No signature forgery or code execution is claimed. Reviewed commit: a625e0dff5ee8376035d80c05b72addae5f4aef1.

CLI HD derivation silently discards accepted path hardening and derives different key material. Locations: core/HdPath.ts:48-75 and :95-125 (parseSegment/parseHdPath), core/Hd.ts:94-101 (deriveNode honors childIndex), and cli/commands/hd.ts:277-293 (derive subcommand reconstructs an account path). parseHdPath accepts hardened change/index segments, but cmdHd takes only parsed.profile/account/change/index and calls Identity.fromAccount, whose formatHdPath reconstructs non-hardened change/index segments. Reproduction: requested path m/ebp'/dilithium'/0'/0/7' is accepted, yet the actual CLI derive branch saves provenance for m/ebp'/dilithium'/0'/0/7. Executing actual deriveNode and deriveAccountNode with the same fixed 64-byte seed produces different node keys for these paths. The harness used actual path/HD code with Node crypto.hkdfSync implementing the imported SHA-512 HKDF primitive; the CLI Identity constructor was stubbed to expose its actual chosen path without generating PQ keys or storing real private material. The command completed normally and saved the reconstructed path. A user recording the requested path for recovery therefore has instructions for different key material. Numeric profile forms can similarly bypass the named-profile hardening check. Canonical supported paths remain unaffected; malformed or unsupported hardening should not silently become another accepted derivation. Reviewed commit: 751c7fa6440a27a6d75369a97919f2c3ea154a47.

HD command numeric options accept trailing garbage and silently select different indices or accounts. Location: cli/commands/hd.ts:45-60 (numberArg), used by new-identity, generate-mnemonic and discover. numberArg uses Number.parseInt and validates only the resulting nonnegative integer, rather than requiring the entire option to be a valid integer. Reproduction against the actual helper: account='1e3' returns 1, account='7garbage' returns 7, and account='3.9' returns 3. The same helper handles index and gap-limit. A typo or malformed automation input can therefore derive a different deterministic identity or change recovery scan limits instead of rejecting the request. Node 24 type-stripped execution confirmed these return values; no actual keys or files were created for this check. Out-of-range integer checks later in core derivation do not catch these already-truncated, in-range values. This is distinct from the accepted-path hardening issue: it affects numeric CLI options even when the resulting canonical path has no hardening ambiguity. Reviewed commit: 751c7fa6440a27a6d75369a97919f2c3ea154a47.

HD discovery counts server failures as unused identities and can stop before published identities. Location: cli/commands/hd.ts:203-257 (discoverLocal), especially serverFound=res.ok at :240 and gap increment in the no-match branch. For each derived fingerprint the scanner treats every non-2xx response as absent, including HTTP 429 and 503. Those failures consume the gap limit and produce a successful but incomplete scan. Reproduction against actual discoverLocal: no local identities, gapLimit=2, server stubs returning 503 for indices 0 and 1 and 200 for index 2. The function requests only 0 and 1, returns normally without any discovery output, and never checks the published index 2. Fingerprint generation and local enumeration were stubbed; actual loop, fetch-status classification and gap logic ran under Node 24. The current server distinguishes an absent identity with HTTP 400 'unknown subject', so an unavailable-service response is not proof of an unused slot. A network exception does abort via the outer command catch; this flaw concerns unsuccessful HTTP responses that resolve normally. With the default limit, an outage or rate-limit burst can silently exhaust 20 slots and conceal recoverable identities. Reviewed commit: 751c7fa6440a27a6d75369a97919f2c3ea154a47.

CLI contact fetch drops server verification and revocation metadata when writing the shared contact file. Locations: cli/commands/server.ts:175-213 (response projection in cmdFetchIdentity) and :243-247 (saved contact JSON), versus server/handlers/identity.ts:267-284 (identity endpoint emits metadata). The CLI constructs an ExternalIdentity with keys, variants and details only, dropping detailsMeta, revoked, revokedDetails and revocationCertificate. Fetching or refreshing a contact through the CLI therefore removes email-endorsement information and revocation status supplied by the server, including from a contact also used by the GUI. Reproduction with the actual cmdFetchIdentity: a synthetic successful identity response includes a verified email claim plus revocation metadata; the written JSON contains none of those four metadata fields. Actual matchVerifiedEmailIdentities reports a unique match for an active source record with verified detailsMeta, but none for the CLI-saved projection. Node 24 evaluated actual fetch/projection and shared matching functions with an in-memory filesystem; key validation was stubbed to isolate metadata handling, not to test cryptographic validity. Real valid keys follow the same projection. This demonstrates lost metadata and degraded client interpretation, not a claim that the reproduction forged a verified email or bypassed signature checks. It is distinct from issue #12's stale opaque-value cache retention. Reviewed commit: 751c7fa6440a27a6d75369a97919f2c3ea154a47.

Server-directory CLI output emits untrusted terminal control sequences verbatim. Locations: cli/commands/server.ts:261-290 (asServerEntry preserves remote detail strings) and :376-392 (cmdListServerIdentities prints path/value), with server/handlers/identity.ts:313-325 and server/body.ts:121 onward accepting arbitrary length-bounded detail strings. A published detail can contain ESC/ANSI controls, and the directory listing inserts those strings directly into console output; the variable named safeValue only distinguishes string versus JSON representation and performs no escaping. Reproduction against actual cmdListServerIdentities: return a directory entry whose name detail starts with the erase-screen sequence U+001B followed by '[2J' and display text. A captured console.log string contains that sequence unchanged. Actual validateStringLength also accepts this detail value. The test captured strings and never emitted terminal controls to the tool output or exercised a real terminal. Terminal behavior depends on the emulator, but ordinary ANSI-aware terminals can have displayed content cleared or rewritten by such output, obscuring identity listings or spoofing what the user sees. No shell-command execution, clipboard access or real malicious server is claimed. This is separate from the historical password-echo finding. Reviewed commit: 751c7fa6440a27a6d75369a97919f2c3ea154a47.
